items.title: Albert Jiles Interview, 1960-06-15
items.q: So we made up a band with Lawrence Toker, Melvin Frank, Bill Hamilton. He was a banjo player. We made up a little band and we began to play together, or rehearsing, not playing a job.

ctx.x: After you studied, say a couple of years, when did you start playing any jobs with the real band, not necessarily professional, or that is to get paid for, but when did you join any small group or brass band? Can you remember what you'd say is your first job or your first orchestra?

Well, after I got the drum, as I told you, my uncle got the drum from a forum shop. I was going to Lansing. I had a fellow come to bring society notice to my house. His name was Lawrence Randall. He said, I told him I had a drum. He said, well, I got a trumpet. I'm learning how to play music. He said, I'm thinking about going to Old Man Chalini. And I told him it was a good idea to go over there. And so he said, of course, I've been getting a little lessons from my uncle, Joe Nicholas. I said, yeah? I said, yeah.…
I don't want to interrupt you, but I'll never think of it again. How was Faiso as a drummer?

items.title: Albert Jiles Interview, 1961-02-24
items.q: A fellow they called Melvin Frank. He's a clarinet player. He did. And Bill Hamilton. He's living. He don't play anymore. He's a bass player and a banjo player. But we four took over the job.

ctx.x: or nothing. And that's a bass player? You have any bass player? No, we didn't have any bass player.

No bass, piano? No piano player. I see. Well that's the first band I started playing with. After my uncle took me to Old Man's Shalow there. That was the first band. And on the way from that house I met Chris Kelly, he was playing Lawn Party and Faye Soda drummer, that was a guy I admired too, was a great drummer. And he asked me to help him carry his drum while he was playing. And so I was telling him, I was going to less and taking up drums. I'll let you work out tonight. So I got on the drum and started…
I thought maybe that song had something to do with Marcus Garvey, you know. No. Because he was a Jew maker too, you know.
